Two nodes can be alike without being linked. Two customers who buy the same products, two papers
that cite the same sources, or two proteins that bind the same partners are similar because of the
company they keep. Measures of node similarity put a number on this idea, and they have a direct
practical use: a pair of nodes with much in common but no link between them is a good candidate for
a link that is missing or about to form. This page covers similarity between nodes, link
prediction, the prediction of missing node attributes, and, at the end, the comparison of whole
graphs: isomorphism, symmetry, pattern matching, and edit distance.

## Neighborhood similarity

The simplest measures compare the neighbors of two nodes. Taking the karate club's two leaders, the
instructor (ID 1) and the administrator (ID 34), [`get_common_neighbors()`](../reference/Graph.get_common_neighbors.qmd)
lists the members who are friends with both:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

karate = ec.karate_club()
karate.get_common_neighbors(1, 34)
```

Four members are friends with both leaders. Whether four is many depends on how many friends each
has, so most measures normalize the count. The *Jaccard coefficient* divides the number of shared
neighbors by the number of distinct neighbors of either node, which gives a score between 0 (no
neighbors in common) and 1 (identical neighborhoods).
[`jaccard_coefficient()`](../reference/Graph.jaccard_coefficient.qmd) scores a list of pairs,
given as IDs or labels, and returns `(u, v, score)` triples:

```{python}
karate.jaccard_coefficient([(1, 34), (1, 2), (33, 34)])
```

The two leaders share only 14% of their combined friends, while the instructor and member `"1"`
(ID 2) share 39%. The administrator and member `"32"` (ID 33) are the most alike of the three
pairs, with more than half of their friends in common.

To compare every pair at once, [`jaccard_similarity()`](../reference/Graph.jaccard_similarity.qmd)
returns a nested dictionary keyed by node ID. Sorting one node's row ranks the others by how much
they resemble it:

```{python}
jaccard = karate.jaccard_similarity()
ranked = sorted(jaccard[34].items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
[(karate.get_label_from_id(node), round(score, 3)) for node, score in ranked[1:6]]
```

The first entry, the administrator's similarity of 1 with itself, is skipped. After member `"32"`
comes member `"2"` (ID 3), who belongs to the instructor's faction but has many friends in the
administrator's, then two members of the administrator's faction, and finally the instructor.

Four neighborhood measures are available in this all-pairs form. They differ in how they normalize
the number of shared neighbors, written here as `c` for two nodes with `k_u` and `k_v` neighbors:

| Method | Score |
|---|---|
| [`jaccard_similarity()`](../reference/Graph.jaccard_similarity.qmd) | `c / (k_u + k_v - c)`, shared neighbors over all distinct neighbors |
| [`dice_similarity()`](../reference/Graph.dice_similarity.qmd) | `2c / (k_u + k_v)` |
| [`cosine_similarity()`](../reference/Graph.cosine_similarity.qmd) | `c / sqrt(k_u k_v)` |
| [`overlap_similarity()`](../reference/Graph.overlap_similarity.qmd) | `c / min(k_u, k_v)`, which is 1 whenever one neighborhood contains the other |

All four rank pairs in a similar order. The overlap coefficient stands apart, because it measures
containment: a member with three friends, all of whom are also friends of a leader, has an overlap
of 1 with that leader. For a matrix over a chosen set of nodes, in a known order,
[`pairwise_similarity()`](../reference/Graph.pairwise_similarity.qmd) takes a list of nodes
and a `method=` (`"jaccard"`, `"dice"`, `"cosine"`, or `"invlogweighted"`, the Adamic–Adar index
described below):

```{python}
leaders = [1, 2, 33, 34]
matrix = karate.pairwise_similarity(leaders, method="cosine")
[[round(value, 2) for value in row] for row in matrix]
```

The matrix has two blocks. The instructor and member `"1"` resemble each other, as do the
administrator and member `"32"`, but there is little resemblance across the two pairs.

[`topological_overlap()`](../reference/Graph.topological_overlap.qmd) computes a related measure,
the topological overlap used in gene co-expression analysis (WGCNA). It is close to the overlap
coefficient, but also counts a direct link between the two nodes, and so suits networks in which
linked nodes with shared neighbors form modules.

### Structural equivalence

Two nodes with exactly the same neighbors are *structurally equivalent*: they occupy the same
position in the network, and any measure that depends only on the structure gives them the same
value. A Jaccard similarity of 1 finds them:

```{python}
equivalent = [
    (karate.get_label_from_id(u), karate.get_label_from_id(v))
    for u, row in jaccard.items()
    for v, score in row.items()
    if u < v and score == 1.0
]
equivalent
```

Members `"14"`, `"15"`, `"18"`, `"20"`, and `"22"` are all friends with exactly the same two
people, members `"32"` and `"33"`, and so are interchangeable; so are members `"17"` and `"21"`,
whose only friends are the instructor and member `"1"`. Structural equivalence is strict, and most
large networks contain few exactly equivalent pairs, which is why graded measures such as those
above are used to find nodes that are *nearly* equivalent. The section on
[symmetries](#symmetries) below describes a broader kind of equivalence.

## Link prediction

Link prediction asks which of the pairs that are not linked are most likely to be linked: friends
that a social network should suggest, interactions that a biologist should test in the laboratory,
or links in a partially observed network that are probably present but were missed. The usual
approach scores every unlinked pair and ranks the pairs by score.

EdgeCase has six scoring methods. Each takes an optional list of pairs as `ebunch=` and, when it is
left out, scores every pair of nodes that are not already linked:

| Method | Score for nodes `u` and `v` | Idea |
|---|---|---|
| [`common_neighbors()`](../reference/Graph.common_neighbors.qmd) | the number of shared neighbors | friends of friends become friends |
| [`jaccard_coefficient()`](../reference/Graph.jaccard_coefficient.qmd) | shared neighbors over all distinct neighbors | normalizes for popularity |
| [`adamic_adar_index()`](../reference/Graph.adamic_adar_index.qmd) | the sum of `1 / log(k)` over shared neighbors of degree `k` | a shared neighbor with few contacts is stronger evidence than a hub |
| [`resource_allocation_index()`](../reference/Graph.resource_allocation_index.qmd) | the sum of `1 / k` over shared neighbors | like Adamic–Adar, with a steeper penalty for hubs |
| [`preferential_attachment()`](../reference/Graph.preferential_attachment.qmd) | `k_u × k_v` | well-connected nodes attract new links |
| [`common_neighbor_centrality()`](../reference/Graph.common_neighbor_centrality.qmd) | shared neighbors plus a bonus for nodes that are close | helps pairs with no shared neighbors |

Applied to the karate club, the resource allocation index picks out these pairs as the most likely
missing friendships:

```{python}
scores = karate.resource_allocation_index()
top = sorted(scores, key=lambda triple: triple[2], reverse=True)[:5]
[(karate.get_label_from_id(u), karate.get_label_from_id(v), round(score, 3)) for u, v, score in top]
```

The `scores` list holds all 483 unlinked pairs. At the top is member `"2"` and the administrator,
the same pair that stood out in the Jaccard ranking above: member `"2"` has many friends in common
with the administrator despite belonging to the other faction. Next come pairs that join each
leader to a close associate of the other.

The methods differ in what they reward, and the differences show at the top of their rankings. The
Jaccard coefficient favors pairs of low-degree nodes whose few neighbors coincide, so its highest
scores go to the structurally equivalent members found above, each pair sharing both of its two
friends. The resource allocation index favors pairs that share many neighbors with few contacts of
their own.

### Evaluating predictors

The way to choose among the methods for a particular network is to test them. A standard test
hides some of the edges, scores the pairs of the remaining graph, and checks whether the hidden
edges score higher than the pairs that were never linked. The jazz musicians network (simplified,
since it has duplicate edges) is large enough for a meaningful test. Here 10% of its edges are held
out at random:

```{python}
import random

full = ec.jazz().simplify()
edges = [(source, target) for _, source, target in full.get_edges_as_tuples()]
held_out = random.Random(1).sample(edges, len(edges) // 10)

train = ec.jazz().simplify()
for source, target in held_out:
    train.delete_edge(source, target)

full.count_edges(), train.count_edges()
```

[`get_edges_as_tuples()`](../reference/Graph.get_edges_as_tuples.qmd) returns `(id, source,
target)` triples, and the training graph is built by loading the network a second time and
deleting the held-out edges with [`delete_edge()`](../reference/Graph.delete_edge.qmd).

Two summaries of a ranking are common. The *AUC* is the probability that a randomly chosen
held-out edge scores higher than a randomly chosen pair that was never linked; 0.5 is no better
than chance and 1 is perfect. *Precision* is the fraction of the top-ranked pairs, as many as there
are held-out edges, that really are held-out edges. A function that computes both from a list of
scores, with the help of Polars:

```{python}
missing = pl.DataFrame(
    {"u": [min(edge) for edge in held_out], "v": [max(edge) for edge in held_out], "missing": True}
)


def evaluate(scores):
    table = (
        pl.DataFrame(scores, schema=["u", "v", "score"], orient="row")
        .with_columns(u=pl.min_horizontal("u", "v"), v=pl.max_horizontal("u", "v"))
        .join(missing, on=["u", "v"], how="left")
        .with_columns(pl.col("missing").fill_null(False))
    )
    n_pos = table["missing"].sum()
    n_neg = table.height - n_pos
    rank_sum = table["score"].rank("average").filter(table["missing"]).sum()
    return {
        "auc": round((rank_sum - n_pos * (n_pos + 1) / 2) / (n_pos * n_neg), 3),
        "precision": round(table.sort("score", descending=True).head(n_pos)["missing"].mean(), 3),
    }
```

Each pair is put in a standard order, smaller ID first, so that it can be matched against the
held-out edges. The AUC comes from the ranks of the scores, which is equivalent to comparing every
held-out edge with every unlinked pair, and ties count as half. Running each predictor on the
training graph:

```{python}
predictors = [
    "common_neighbors",
    "jaccard_coefficient",
    "adamic_adar_index",
    "resource_allocation_index",
    "preferential_attachment",
]
pl.DataFrame([{"method": name, **evaluate(getattr(train, name)())} for name in predictors])
```

The four methods based on shared neighbors all do well, with an AUC above 0.95. About half of their
top 274 predictions are edges that were held out, against fewer than 2% for a random guess, since
only 274 of the 17,035 unlinked pairs are held-out edges. The resource allocation index is
slightly ahead, a result that holds in many studies of real networks. Preferential attachment is
far behind: in this network, being popular says much less about whom a musician played with than
having partners in common does.

A few cautions apply to this kind of test. A single random split gives a noisy estimate, so repeat
it with several seeds before drawing fine distinctions. Holding out edges can disconnect nodes, and
an isolated node gets a score of zero with everyone. And when the network grows over time, holding
out the most recent edges gives a more honest test than holding out random ones.

### Using communities

Links are more likely inside communities than between them, and three predictors use a community
attribute to sharpen their scores. [`cn_soundarajan_hopcroft()`](../reference/Graph.cn_soundarajan_hopcroft.qmd)
and [`ra_index_soundarajan_hopcroft()`](../reference/Graph.ra_index_soundarajan_hopcroft.qmd) give
extra weight to shared neighbors in the pair's own community, and
[`within_inter_cluster()`](../reference/Graph.within_inter_cluster.qmd) compares the shared
neighbors inside the pair's community with those outside it. The communities are read from a node
attribute, `community` by default, such as one written by a detection method (see
[Community detection](14-communities.qmd)):

```{python}
train.cmty_louvain()

community_predictors = [
    "cn_soundarajan_hopcroft",
    "ra_index_soundarajan_hopcroft",
    "within_inter_cluster",
]
pl.DataFrame(
    [
        {"method": name, **evaluate(getattr(train, name)(community="cmty_louvain"))}
        for name in community_predictors
    ]
)
```

On the jazz network the community information doesn't help. `ra_index_soundarajan_hopcroft()` and
`within_inter_cluster()` give a score of zero to every pair that spans two communities, and many of
the held-out edges do. `cn_soundarajan_hopcroft()`, which keeps the plain count for such pairs, does
about as well as `common_neighbors()` but no better. Whether communities help
depends on how sharply they divide a network, which is a good reason to run a test like this one
before relying on any predictor.

## Similarity from paths

Neighborhood measures only see two steps from a node: pairs that share no neighbors all score
zero. *SimRank* extends the idea recursively, with the rule that two nodes are similar if their
neighbors are similar. [`simrank_similarity()`](../reference/Graph.simrank_similarity.qmd)
returns the score of one pair when given two nodes, one node's scores against every other when
given one, and the full table when given none:

```{python}
simrank = karate.simrank_similarity(source=34)
ranked = sorted(simrank.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
[(karate.get_label_from_id(node), round(score, 3)) for node, score in ranked[1:6]]
```

Member `"32"` is again the administrator's closest match, followed by members whose friends
resemble the administrator's friends. SimRank scores spread over a narrower range than Jaccard
scores, because similarity propagates through the whole network, discounted at each step by the
`importance_factor=` (0.9 by default). [`simrank_star_similarity()`](../reference/Graph.simrank_star_similarity.qmd)
is a variant that counts paths of every length, which corrects SimRank's habit of scoring zero for
nodes at an odd distance from one another in nearly bipartite graphs.

SimRank compares every pair of nodes, which is costly on large graphs. *Panther* estimates
similarity by sampling short random paths and counting how often two nodes appear on the same
path, which makes it fast enough for large networks. [`panther_similarity()`](../reference/Graph.panther_similarity.qmd)
returns the `k` nodes most similar to a source:

```{python}
panther = karate.panther_similarity(34, k=5, seed=1)
{karate.get_label_from_id(node): round(score, 3) for node, score in panther.items()}
```

The scores are estimates, so use `seed=` for repeatable results; a different seed gives the same
leader but can change the order further down. [`panther_vector_similarity()`](../reference/Graph.panther_vector_similarity.qmd)
compares nodes by their profiles of path counts instead.

## Predicting node attributes

Similarity also helps to fill in missing node attributes. If only some nodes are labelled with a
category, the categories of the rest can be inferred from their positions in the network, on the
assumption that linked nodes tend to share a category. This is *semi-supervised* learning: a few
labelled examples, together with the structure, guide the predictions for everything else.

[`harmonic_function()`](../reference/Graph.harmonic_function.qmd) spreads the known categories
through the network until each node's prediction agrees with those of its neighbors. As a test,
suppose that only the two leaders' sides were known. The categories go into a node attribute that
is set for those two nodes only:

```{python}
karate.set_node_attrs("side", {1: "instructor", 34: "administrator"})
predicted = karate.harmonic_function(label_name="side")

faction = karate.get_node_attrs("faction")
correct = sum((predicted[node] == "instructor") == (faction[node] == 1) for node in predicted)
correct, karate.count_nodes()
```

Nodes without a value for the attribute are treated as unlabelled, and `predicted` gives a category
for every node. From the two leaders alone, the method assigns all 34 members to the faction they
actually joined when the club split, which the `faction` attribute records.
[`local_and_global_consistency()`](../reference/Graph.local_and_global_consistency.qmd) is a
variant that allows the known categories to be overruled when the network strongly disagrees with
them, which helps when some of the known labels may be wrong; its `alpha=` sets how much weight the
network gets.

## Comparing graphs

The rest of this page compares whole graphs rather than nodes: whether two graphs have the same
structure, where a pattern occurs in a graph, and how much two graphs differ.

### Isomorphism

Two graphs are *isomorphic* when their nodes can be matched up so that every edge of one becomes an
edge of the other. They are then the same graph, drawn or numbered differently. The Petersen graph,
for example, is also the *Kneser graph* K(5, 2), whose nodes are the pairs from a set of five
items, linked when the pairs have no item in common.
[`is_isomorphic()`](../reference/Graph.is_isomorphic.qmd) confirms it, and
[`find_isomorphism()`](../reference/Graph.find_isomorphism.qmd) returns the correspondence, from
node IDs of the first graph to node IDs of the second:

```{python}
petersen = ec.Graph().add_named_graph("petersen")
kneser = ec.Graph().add_kneser_graph(n=5, k=2)

mapping = petersen.find_isomorphism(kneser)
pairs = {node: kneser.get_label_from_id(image) for node, image in mapping.items()}
petersen.is_isomorphic(kneser), pairs
```

Each of the Kneser graph's nodes is labelled by its pair, so the mapping shows which pair each node
of the Petersen graph corresponds to. Both methods take `node_attr=` and `edge_attr=`, which
require matched nodes and edges to agree on the given attributes. That turns the question into
whether two labelled structures, such as two molecules with atom types, are the same.

Deciding isomorphism can be expensive in the worst case, and two cheaper checks help when many
graphs must be compared. [`could_be_isomorphic()`](../reference/Graph.could_be_isomorphic.qmd)
compares simple invariants, such as the degrees and triangle counts, and returns `False` when they
rule an isomorphism out. [`weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash()`](../reference/Graph.weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash.qmd)
computes a hash that isomorphic graphs always share, which makes it a fast way to group a large
collection of graphs into candidate classes. The hash is not a proof, though: some graphs that are
not isomorphic share it. The complete bipartite graph K(3, 3) and the triangular prism are both
3-regular graphs on six nodes, and the hash can't tell them apart:

```{python}
k33 = ec.Graph().add_complete_bipartite_graph(n1=3, n2=3)
prism = ec.Graph().add_prism_graph(n=3)

(
    k33.weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash() == prism.weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash(),
    k33.could_be_isomorphic(prism),
    k33.is_isomorphic(prism),
)
```

The hashes agree, but the prism contains two triangles and K(3, 3) has none, which is enough for
`could_be_isomorphic()` to rule out an isomorphism. A hash that matches always needs to be confirmed
with `is_isomorphic()`. For an exact canonical form, [`canonical_labeling()`](../reference/Graph.canonical_labeling.qmd)
numbers the nodes so that isomorphic graphs, renumbered, become identical.
[`weisfeiler_lehman_subgraph_hashes()`](../reference/Graph.weisfeiler_lehman_subgraph_hashes.qmd)
gives each node a hash of its neighborhood at each round, which serves as a set of structural
features for machine learning.

### Symmetries

An isomorphism from a graph onto itself is an *automorphism*, a symmetry of the graph.
[`automorphism_cosets()`](../reference/Graph.automorphism_cosets.qmd) describes them compactly: for
each node, in ID order, it lists the nodes that the node can be sent to by a symmetry that keeps
every smaller node in place. The product of the list lengths is the number of symmetries. The
Petersen graph is famously symmetric:

```{python}
import math

cosets = petersen.automorphism_cosets()
math.prod(len(coset) for coset in cosets.values())
```

It has 120 symmetries, and since its first node can be sent to any of the ten, every node is
equivalent to every other. Applied to the karate club, the cosets show which members are
interchangeable:

```{python}
cosets = karate.automorphism_cosets()
symmetries = math.prod(len(coset) for coset in cosets.values())
interchangeable = [
    [karate.get_label_from_id(node) for node in coset]
    for coset in cosets.values()
    if len(coset) > 1
]
symmetries, interchangeable
```

The 480 symmetries come from three groups of interchangeable members. Two are the groups of
structurally equivalent members found earlier. The five members `"14"`, `"15"`, `"18"`, `"20"`, and
`"22"` appear in a shrinking chain of lists: any of the five can take the first place, then any of
the remaining four the second, and so on, for 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 = 120 orderings. Members `"17"` and
`"21"` double that number. The third group, the pair `"4"` and `"10"`, is new and doubles it
again. These two members don't have the same friends, so they aren't structurally
equivalent, but swapping them along with their friends `"5"` and `"6"` leaves the network
unchanged. Nodes related by a symmetry are *automorphically equivalent*, a weaker condition than
structural equivalence.

### Finding patterns

[`subgraph_isomorphisms()`](../reference/Graph.subgraph_isomorphisms.qmd) finds the places where a
small pattern graph occurs inside a larger one, and returns one mapping per occurrence, from
pattern node IDs to node IDs of the larger graph. With `symmetry=True`, occurrences that differ
only by a symmetry of the pattern, such as the six ways of matching the corners of a triangle, are
reported once:

```{python}
square = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(n=4)

induced = karate.subgraph_isomorphisms(square, symmetry=True)
any_square = karate.subgraph_isomorphisms(square, induced=False, symmetry=True)
len(induced), len(any_square)
```

By default the occurrences are *induced*: the four members must be linked around a square with no
diagonal friendships, which happens 36 times. With `induced=False`, extra edges are allowed, and
any four members with friendships around a square count, including those that also have one or
both diagonals; there are 154 of these. `limit=` stops the search after a given number of
occurrences, and [`is_subgraph_isomorphic()`](../reference/Graph.is_subgraph_isomorphic.qmd) only
asks whether there is at least one. The same `node_attr=` and `edge_attr=` options make the search
match attributes as well as structure, which is how a query such as "a person who works at a
company that is based in Berlin" is matched in a knowledge graph.
[`largest_common_subgraph()`](../reference/Graph.largest_common_subgraph.qmd) finds the largest
induced subgraphs that two graphs share.

### Measuring differences

When two graphs describe the same nodes, such as two snapshots of a network or a network and a
reconstruction of it, the question is how much they differ. As an example, here is a copy of the
karate club with two friendships removed and one added:

```{python}
before = ec.karate_club()
after = ec.karate_club()
after.delete_edge("0", "1").delete_edge("32", "33").add_edge("0", "33")

before.edge_overlap(after)
```

[`edge_overlap()`](../reference/Graph.edge_overlap.qmd) matches edges by the labels of their
endpoints. The two graphs share 76 edges, two are only in the first, and one is only in the second,
for a Jaccard index of 0.96. [`differential_edges()`](../reference/Graph.differential_edges.qmd)
lists the edges that differ:

```{python}
before.differential_edges(after)
```

[`graph_edit_distance()`](../reference/Graph.graph_edit_distance.qmd) counts the node and edge
insertions and deletions needed to turn one graph into the other. By default it also matches nodes
by label, which makes it fast:

```{python}
before.graph_edit_distance(after)
```

When the nodes of the two graphs don't correspond, `exact=True` searches over all possible
correspondences for the cheapest sequence of edits. A five-node cycle becomes a six-node path by
deleting one edge and adding one node and one edge:

```{python}
cycle = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(n=5)
path = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(n=6)
cycle.graph_edit_distance(path, exact=True)["distance"]
```

The exact search grows quickly with the size of the graphs, and is practical only for graphs of up
to a dozen or so nodes. The exact mode accepts functions that set the cost of each kind of edit,
and `timeout=` and `upper_bound=` limit the search.
[`optimize_graph_edit_distance()`](../reference/Graph.optimize_graph_edit_distance.qmd) yields
better and better estimates as it runs, which is useful when an approximate answer is enough, and
[`optimal_edit_paths()`](../reference/Graph.optimal_edit_paths.qmd) returns the edits themselves.

## Choosing a method

| Question | Methods |
|---|---|
| Which nodes have similar neighbors? | `jaccard_similarity()`, `cosine_similarity()`, `dice_similarity()`, `overlap_similarity()`, `pairwise_similarity()` |
| Which nodes are similar beyond their immediate neighbors? | `simrank_similarity()`, `simrank_star_similarity()`, `panther_similarity()` |
| Which missing links are most likely? | `resource_allocation_index()`, `adamic_adar_index()`, `common_neighbors()`, `jaccard_coefficient()`, and the community-aware variants |
| What are the missing categories of some nodes? | `harmonic_function()`, `local_and_global_consistency()` |
| Are two graphs the same? | `is_isomorphic()`, `find_isomorphism()`, `could_be_isomorphic()`, `weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash()`, `canonical_labeling()` |
| Which nodes are interchangeable? | `automorphism_cosets()`, a Jaccard similarity of 1 |
| Where does a pattern occur? | `subgraph_isomorphisms()`, `is_subgraph_isomorphic()`, `motif_census()` |
| How much do two graphs differ? | `edge_overlap()`, `differential_edges()`, `graph_edit_distance()` |

Counting every small pattern in a graph, rather than searching for one, is the subject of
[Clustering and motifs](15-clustering-and-motifs.qmd#motifs).
